etymology: From the Hebrew people; the New Testament epistle written to Jewish-Christian readers, anonymously, ~AD 60-70.
biblical_def: The New Testament epistle anonymously addressed to Hebrew-Christian readers wavering under persecution; presents Christ as superior to angels, Moses, the Levitical priesthood, and the old covenant; the great superiority-of-Christ argument.
webster_summary: NT epistle: Christ superior to all the old covenant.
webster_full: The anonymous New Testament epistle written to Hebrew-Christian readers tempted to revert to Judaism under persecution; argues from the Old Testament that Christ is superior to angels, Moses, Aaron, and the entire Levitical sacrificial system; develops the Melchizedek priesthood, the new covenant, and the once-for-all atonement; climaxes in Hebrews 11's roll of faith and Hebrews 12's exhortation to endure.
scriptures: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross.
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
corruption_summary: Read piecemeal for individual verses; the cumulative argument that Christ is greater than all is the book's spine.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews makes one sustained argument: Christ is greater. Greater than angels, than Moses, than Aaron, than the old covenant, than the sacrifices. Reading the book in pieces misses the cumulative weight. Read it whole — then you see why the readers must not turn back.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ivri — Hebrew, descendant of Eber.
usage: Read Hebrews whole, not piecemeal.
The argument is Christ-superior.

etymology: Composite term for the eschatological day of final divine judgment.
biblical_def: The eschatological day when Christ judges the living and the dead — the great white throne (Rev 20:11-15), the bema seat (2 Cor 5:10), the day of wrath and revelation of righteous judgment (Rom 2:5-6).
webster_summary: Christ's final judgment of the living and the dead.
webster_full: The eschatological day on which Christ, the appointed Judge, will judge the living and the dead — wicked at the great white throne, believers at the bema seat for reward; the day of wrath against the impenitent and of vindication for the faithful; the climax of all human history.
scriptures: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened... and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books.

But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; Who will render to every man according to his deeds.
corruption_summary: Either denied (universalism) or commercialized (apocalyptic kitsch); Scripture treats it as the sober anchor of moral seriousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Judgment Day is real, certain, and individual. Every life will stand before Christ. The denial of judgment removes the gravity from morality; the commercialization removes the holiness. Recover the day as Scripture frames it: certain, sober, and met by the gospel.
usage: Live in light of Judgment Day.
Both the wicked and the believer face the bema.

etymology: Composite of Messianic + prophecy; the Old Testament foretelling of the coming Anointed One.
biblical_def: The Old Testament prophecies foretelling the coming Messiah — His person, work, suffering, and reign — fulfilled in Jesus Christ; collected and developed across Genesis through Malachi.
webster_summary: OT prophecies of the coming Messiah fulfilled in Jesus.
webster_full: The body of Old Testament prophecy foretelling the coming Messiah — the seed of the woman (Gen 3:15), of Abraham (Gen 12:3), of Judah (Gen 49:10), of David (2 Sam 7); the Suffering Servant (Isa 53), the pierced one (Zech 12:10), the Branch, the Son of Man (Dan 7), the King on Zion (Ps 2). Fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.
Search the scriptures... they are they which testify of me.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a list of proof-texts rather than received as the Old Testament's coherent Christ-witness.
corruption_paragraphs: Messianic prophecy is not a list — it is a development. Genesis names the seed; Abraham specifies; Judah narrows; David crowns; the prophets fill in suffering, reign, and return. Read the whole arc, not isolated verses. The Old Testament is one long Messianic prophecy.
usage: Read the OT as one Messianic arc.
Christ said the prophets testify of Him.

etymology: Composite term for the biblical view of marriage as covenant before God.
biblical_def: Marriage understood as covenant — sworn before God, between one man and one woman, lifelong, exclusive, image of Christ and the church (Mal 2:14-16; Eph 5:31-32; Matt 19:4-6).
webster_summary: Marriage as lifelong covenant before God.
webster_full: The biblical understanding of marriage as covenant — sworn before God between one man and one woman, lifelong, exclusive, ordered toward children, family discipleship, and image of Christ and the church; distinguished from contractual or sentimental views.
scriptures: Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
corruption_summary: Replaced by contractual or sentimental marriage; Scripture's covenant view holds the lifelong, image-bearing weight.
corruption_paragraphs: Covenant marriage is the ground of biblical family. Not contract (which expires), not sentiment (which fades), but covenant (which binds). Christ took it as image of His own self-giving to the church. Recover the weight; the gospel itself depends on getting marriage's image right.
usage: Recover marriage as covenant.
Christ-and-church image hangs on it.

etymology: Acts 15 — the apostolic council of ~AD 49 settling the Gentile-inclusion question.
biblical_def: The first apostolic council (Acts 15, ~AD 49) gathered to settle whether Gentile converts must be circumcised; ruled they need not, issuing the Apostolic Decree; foundational pattern for ecclesial decision-making.
webster_full: The first apostolic council, gathered in Jerusalem (~AD 49) to settle the question whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep Mosaic law; concluded — through testimony, Scripture, and Spirit-led discernment — they need not, issuing the Apostolic Decree to facilitate table-fellowship; foundational pattern for ecclesial decision-making.
scriptures: And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter... but we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.
Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God.
It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.
corruption_summary: Treated as historical curiosity; missing how it shaped all subsequent ecclesial conciliarism (Nicaea, Chalcedon, etc.).
corruption_paragraphs: The Jerusalem Council established the pattern: when major doctrinal issues arise, the church gathers — apostles and elders, with testimony, Scripture, and Spirit-discernment — and decides. Nicaea, Chalcedon, Westminster all stand on Acts 15. Conciliarism is biblical.
usage: Read Acts 15 as the conciliar pattern.
Apostles, elders, Scripture, Spirit, decision.

etymology: Greek Laodikeia — Roman provincial city in Asia Minor, ~50 miles east of Ephesus.
biblical_def: The wealthy, complacent Roman city in Asia Minor whose church received the seventh and most severe of Christ's letters in Revelation 3:14-22 — neither hot nor cold, lukewarm, ready to be spit out.
webster_full: The wealthy Roman provincial city in Asia Minor (modern Denizli, Turkey), known for banking, textiles, and eye-salve; recipient of the seventh and most severe of Christ's letters in Revelation 3:14-22 — neither hot nor cold, lukewarm, content with self-sufficiency, blind to spiritual poverty; offered the strongest call: 'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.'
scriptures: I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot... So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth. Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him.
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans.
corruption_summary: Read narrowly as ancient warning; missing how perfectly it diagnoses comfortable Western Christianity.
corruption_paragraphs: Laodicea is the mirror for prosperous Christianity. Wealthy, self-sufficient, blind to spiritual poverty, lukewarm. The cure is humbling — anoint your eyes, buy gold tried in fire, open the door to the One knocking. Read Revelation 3:14-22 over your own church carefully.
usage: Read Revelation 3 over your own church.
Lukewarm is worse than cold.

etymology: Composite term for Jesus' parables specifically about the kingdom of heaven.
biblical_def: The collection of parables Jesus taught about the kingdom of heaven — sower, wheat-and-tares, mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, pearl, dragnet, unforgiving servant, vineyard laborers, ten virgins, talents, sheep-and-goats — revealing the kingdom in mystery form.
webster_summary: Jesus' parables specifically about the kingdom.
webster_full: The collection of parables in which Jesus reveals the kingdom of heaven in mystery form — gathered especially in Matthew 13 and Luke 13-15 — sower, wheat-and-tares, mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, pearl, dragnet, unforgiving servant, laborers in the vineyard, ten virgins, talents, sheep and goats — concealing the kingdom from the proud while opening it to disciples.
scriptures: Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.
And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it. But without a parable spake he not unto them.
All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them.
corruption_summary: Treated as moral fables; Jesus taught them as kingdom-revelation that hides from the proud.
corruption_paragraphs: The parables are not Aesop's. They are revelatory acts. Jesus tells His disciples plainly: these parables hide the kingdom from outsiders and reveal it to insiders. Read them as keys that turn only in soft hearts. The same parable can save or condemn depending on the soil.
usage: Parables hide and reveal at once.
Read them as kingdom-keys.

etymology: Closing chapter of Proverbs, an acrostic poem on the virtuous wife.
biblical_def: The closing chapter of Proverbs, including King Lemuel's mother's instruction (vv 1-9) and the famous acrostic poem of the virtuous wife (vv 10-31) — twenty-two stanzas covering her industry, fear of God, household management, and worth.
webster_summary: Closing chapter; acrostic poem on the virtuous wife.
webster_full: The closing chapter of Proverbs, in two parts: King Lemuel's mother's instruction (vv 1-9) on kingly character — strong drink and bribery refused, the cause of the afflicted defended; and the famous acrostic poem (vv 10-31) of the virtuous wife — twenty-two stanzas, one per Hebrew letter, showcasing her industry, wisdom, kindness, fear of God, and worth far above rubies.
scriptures: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
Strength and honour are her clothing... She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
corruption_summary: Either weaponized as impossible standard against women, or sentimentalized into Mother's Day reading; missing the wisdom-literature genre.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 31 is wisdom poetry, not job description. It is the embodied portrait of the wisdom Lady Folly opposes throughout the book — fear of God lived out in industrious household life. Husbands are to praise her; mothers to embody her in their own seasons; daughters to grow toward her.
usage: Read Proverbs 31 as wisdom poetry.
Fear of the LORD is the root.

biblical_def: Paul's diagnosis of the root from which all kinds of evil grow (1 Tim 6:10) — not money itself but the love of it; the disposition that pierces souls with many sorrows.
webster_summary: Paul's diagnosed root of all kinds of evil.
webster_full: Paul's specific term for the disposition that loves money — not money itself but love of it — naming it as 'the root of all kinds of evil,' a disposition that has caused some to err from the faith and pierce themselves through with many sorrows; a fundamental danger in the heart of even pastors and saints.
scriptures: For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have.
No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: Misquoted as 'money is the root of all evil' (it is the love of money); missing the precise diagnosis.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's verb is precise: phil-argyria, silver-loving. Money is morally neutral; love of it is corrosive. Even pastors and saints fall here. Self-examination: what would I refuse to give up for the kingdom? That is where the love of money has rooted.
usage: Examine yourself for love of money.
Money is neutral; love of it is the root.

biblical_def: The state Paul learned to glory in (2 Cor 12:9-10) because Christ's strength is made perfect in it; not endorsed sin or moral failure but human limitation that drives one to depend on Christ.
webster_summary: Human limitation in which Christ's strength is perfected.
webster_full: The state of human limitation Paul came to glory in after asking three times for relief from his thorn — the Lord's answer: 'My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.' Not endorsed sin or moral failure but the inadequacy that drives one to depend wholly on Christ; the same word for sickness, frailty, and inability.
scriptures: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
corruption_summary: Eliminated from leadership cultures that idolize strength; Paul boasts in weakness because it is where Christ's power rests.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern leadership culture cannot hear Paul's boast. Strong, capable, dynamic — yes; weak — never. Paul inverts: he glories in weakness because that is where Christ's strength rests. The rest culture you do not need; the rest Christ gives you do.
usage: Glory in weakness; Christ's power rests there.
The rest culture you do not need.

biblical_def: King of Judah (~640-609 BC) who became king at age eight; led the great reform after the rediscovery of the law in the temple; destroyed idols and high places; killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho.
webster_summary: Reformer king who destroyed idols and renewed covenant.
webster_full: The king of Judah from age eight, who at sixteen began to seek the God of his father David and at twenty-six purged Judah and Jerusalem of high places, asherah poles, and idolatry; rediscovered the Book of the Law during temple repairs and led a great covenant renewal; died at Megiddo opposing Pharaoh Necho.
scriptures: And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, and walked in all the way of David his father, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left.
And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses.
corruption_summary: Sentimentalized as the boy-king; missing the depth of his reform and the tragedy of his death.
corruption_paragraphs: Josiah is the model reformer-king. His youth did not disqualify him; his courage to dismantle entrenched idolatry remade Judah for a generation. His sudden death at Megiddo is the tragic close — even great reform cannot indefinitely delay judgment when a people will not finally turn. Read his reign whole.
usage: Josiah models reform, not retreat.
Even great reform cannot finally delay judgment.

etymology: Hebrew Yisra'el (יִשְׂרָאֵל) — "strives with God" or "God strives."
biblical_def: The covenant name given to Jacob (Gen 32:28) and to the nation descended from him; the people through whom God brought His Messiah; in the New Testament extended through faith to include Gentile believers (Rom 11; Gal 6:16).
webster_summary: Jacob's covenant name; the covenant nation; the people of God.
webster_full: The covenant name given to Jacob after wrestling with God at Peniel; the name of the nation descended from him through twelve sons; the people through whom God brought His Messiah; in the New Testament extended through faith to include Gentile believers grafted into the olive tree (Rom 11), the 'Israel of God' (Gal 6:16).
scriptures: And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel.
And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.
corruption_summary: Reduced either to ethnic-political nation only or to spiritual-only category; Paul holds both in Romans 9-11.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 9-11 forces nuance. Israel after the flesh; Israel of faith; all Israel saved. The categories cannot be collapsed. Bless ethnic Israel; recognize the believing remnant; pray for the fullness; love the Israel of God across both lines.
usage: Hold Romans 9-11's nuances.
The Israel of God includes faith from all peoples.

etymology: From Latin proclamare "to cry out, declare publicly."
biblical_def: Public announcement; the gospel's primary mode (Mark 1:14-15; Acts 8:5; 1 Cor 1:23); the church's central task is heralding what God has done in Christ.
webster_full: Public announcement; the gospel's primary mode of advance; not advice or instruction but declaration of what has happened — Christ has died, Christ is risen, Christ is coming again; the church's central task is to herald.
scriptures: Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God, And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them.
corruption_summary: Replaced by 'sharing' or 'conversation'; the gospel comes with the sound of trumpet, not the murmur of dialog.
corruption_paragraphs: The gospel is news; news is proclaimed. Modern preaching often softens to dialog or therapy, but the kerygma comes by herald. There is a place for conversation; there is a non-negotiable place for proclamation. Recover the herald's voice.
usage: Recover the herald's voice.
The gospel comes by proclamation.

etymology: Hebrew Baal (בַּעַל) — "lord, master," the Canaanite storm-god.
biblical_def: The chief Canaanite storm-fertility god, perpetual rival of YHWH for Israel's allegiance; opposed by Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18); under whose name many local manifestations existed (Baal-Peor, Baal-Zebub, etc.).
webster_summary: Canaanite storm-god; perpetual rival of YHWH.
webster_full: The chief Canaanite storm and fertility god, perpetual rival of YHWH for Israel's worship; bull-shaped imagery, asherah-pole consort, sexual cult; confronted by Elijah at Mount Carmel ('how long halt ye between two opinions?'); the perpetual idol-temptation through Israel's history.
scriptures: How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.
I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them.
They have built also the high places of Baal, to burn their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal.
corruption_summary: Treated as quaint ancient mythology; Baal worship in its essentials — fertility cult, prosperity-religion, syncretism — recurs in every age.
corruption_paragraphs: Baal recurs. Strip the costume and Baal worship is fertility, prosperity, sex-cult, and syncretism — religion that promises rain in exchange for compromise. Elijah's question is perpetual: how long halt ye between two opinions? Choose the LORD.
usage: Confront the Baals of every age.
Elijah's question is perpetual.

etymology: From Latin moneta — "mint," the temple of Juno Moneta where Roman coins were struck.
biblical_def: The medium of exchange; morally neutral as a tool but deeply tested in its love (1 Tim 6:10), use (Luke 16:9-13), and worship-rivalry with God (Matt 6:24); a constant biblical theme.
webster_summary: Medium of exchange; morally neutral; deeply tested in heart.
webster_full: The medium of exchange — coin or currency — morally neutral as instrument but a perpetual heart-test in Scripture: love of it pierces souls (1 Tim 6:10); use of it must be 'unto the Lord' (Luke 16:9-13); worship of it (Mammon) cannot coexist with worship of God (Matt 6:24).
scriptures: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God.
Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations.
corruption_summary: Either demonized (as if money itself were evil) or sacralized (prosperity gospel); Scripture's careful balance is steward, not slave.
corruption_paragraphs: Money is steward-test, not enemy. Christians are not to fear it (it is a tool) or to love it (it is a rival god). Use it for kingdom; do not let it use you. Jesus spoke about money more than heaven and hell combined; take Him seriously on it.
usage: Be steward, not slave.
Use it for kingdom; do not let it use you.
